title: Same Robot, New Language
goal: Every student writes and runs a Python program that drives a square — in pairs.
label: G9 · S1
text:
every student writes and runs a python program that drives a square — in pairs. open with the grade 8 fair photos, then the year’s premise: same robot, professional tools. mblock’s python mode is a real editor — text, autocomplete, error messages. the first program is deliberately familiar: the square. they’ve built it in blocks (grade 7) and read it in python (grade 8, session 17); today they type it from a blank file. familiar problem + new medium = confidence, not overwhelm. institute pair programming as this year’s standard: driver types, navigator reads ahead and catches errors; swap every 10 minutes. it’s how professionals work and it halves the syntax frustration of week one. also set the error-message culture: an error message is information, not an insult — read it aloud, bottom line first. editor tour: file, run, stop, console, autocomplete. break something on purpose; read the error together. pairs type the square from scratch; run on the robot; swap roles halfway. extension ladder: triangle → hexagon → any-n polygon (the 360/n insight, now as code). on your lesson sheet: one error message you met and what it was telling you. function names below follow mblock’s cyberpi python api; minor names vary by version — the class rule is: trust the editor’s autocomplete. indentationerror and missing colons will dominate today — predict it aloud so nobody feels alone. pairs stay together for the whole python bootcamp unit. square runs from hand-typed python pair-programming roles practiced with a swap at least one error message read, decoded, and fixed by the pair import cyberpi
import mbot2

# our old friend, typed from scratch
for i in range(4):
    mbot2.straight(30)    # cm forward
    mbot2.turn(90)        # degrees right

cyberpi.display.show_label(
    'done!', 24, 'center') both partners write and fix python unaided, and an error message is read as information rather than as a wall. the navigator produced working code after the swap three error messages explained in the pair's own words

title: Sensing in Python
goal: Live sensor values read, displayed and logged — the robot’s senses in text form.
label: G9 · S3
text:
live sensor values read, displayed and logged — the robot’s senses in text form. sensors in python return numbers you can hold in a variable: off = cyberpi.quad_rgb_sensor.get_offset_track(). that one line changes the relationship — in blocks, values flowed invisibly; in python, students capture, print, compare and compute with them. build the classic diagnostic tool first: a loop printing the live readings to the screen ten times a second (a dashboard, and their debugging best friend for the rest of the year). this robot senses the floor and its own wheels — there is no ultrasonic anywhere on the rover, so nothing here measures the air in front of it. two numbers matter all year. the quad rgb reports how far off-centre the line is (an offset, roughly −100…+100): push the robot along a line by hand and watch it swing negative–zero–positive — that number is next week’s error signal. the encoders report how far each motor has turned in degrees: push the robot forward by hand and watch the angle climb — that number is session 9’s ruler. build the dashboard; three live values on screen at once, updating without flicker. threshold play: print ‘marker!’ when the l1 probe sees red — an if on a captured value. line offset explorer: hand-push the robot along a line, watch the offset swing; sketch its meaning. on your lesson sheet: what does offset = −60 mean physically? draw it. function names below follow mblock’s cyberpi python api; minor names vary by version — the class rule is: trust the editor’s autocomplete. str(off) trips everyone — numbers must become text to display; let them hit the error, then explain. calibrate the line sensor first (the grade 7 ritual) or the offset numbers are noise. someone will go looking for the distance sensor: the rover does not carry one, and that absence is the reason session 9 exists. dashboard shows live line offset and encoder angle marker! fires on the red patch and nowhere else team can explain offset’s sign and rough magnitude physically import cyberpi, mbot2, time

mbot2.em_reset_angle('em1')

while true:
    off = cyberpi.quad_rgb_sensor.get_offset_track()
    deg = mbot2.em_get_angle('em1')
    cyberpi.display.show_label(
        'off=' + str(off), 16, 'top')
    cyberpi.display.show_label(
        'deg=' + str(deg), 16, 'center')
    if cyberpi.quad_rgb_sensor.is_color('red', 'l1'):
        cyberpi.display.show_label(
            'marker!', 24, 'bottom')
    time.sleep(0.1) the line offset understood physically — its sign and rough size predicted before the robot is pushed anywhere. offset sign predicted correctly before the robot was pushed the sign convention written where session 6 can find it

title: The Wobble, Explained
goal: Students understand proportional control conceptually — correction proportional to error.
label: G9 · S5
text: students understand proportional control conceptually — correction proportional to error. resurrect grade 7’s board question: why does the line follower zig-zag? now they can answer it. bang-bang control knows only three answers (hard left / straight / hard right) — it always overcorrects, overshoots, and corrects back: the wobble is built into the logic. the fix is one idea: make the correction proportional to the error. slightly off → tiny steering nudge; far off → strong steering. in code it will be one line: steer = error × gain. teach it with the blindfold walk before any code: one student walks a taped line blindfolded; their partner may only say “left”/“right” (bang-bang) — watch them wobble. then allow “a little left” / “way left” (proportional) — the walk visibly smooths. ten minutes of theatre worth a thousand words. then define terms on the board: error (the line offset they measured in session 3), gain (how aggressively we respond), and predict together what too-low gain (drifts off curves) and too-high gain (wobbles again!) will look like tomorrow. blindfold line-walk, bang-bang vs. proportional instructions; debrief what changed. board the model: error → × gain → steering; connect error to session 3’s offset number. paper-trace the algorithm on drawn scenarios: offset −60, gain 0.5 → motors? teams compute by hand. predictions in the lesson sheet: sketch what gain-too-low and gain-too-high trajectories will look like. do not code today — the concept needs its own hour; tomorrow’s implementation then takes minutes. the hand computation (offset × gain → two motor speeds) is the comprehension gate; don’t skip it. class answered the grade 7 wobble question in control terms teams hand-computed motor speeds from offset × gain correctly both failure predictions (low/high gain) sketched the grade 7 wobble question answered in control terms, with motor speeds computed by hand before a single line of code exists. four motor-speed computations correct by hand, with no code written all hour both failure trajectories sketched in advance of any run

title: P-Control
goal: Proportional line following implemented and tuned — the wobble visibly defeated.
label: G9 · S6
text:
proportional line following implemented and tuned — the wobble visibly defeated. implementation day: read the offset, multiply by gain, split the result across the two tracks. the core is genuinely three lines — emphasize that a big idea can be small code. then tuning: start with a low gain, raise it until the robot hugs curves, and keep going until it wobbles again (yesterday’s prediction comes true — applaud it, it means the model is right). tuning protocol is session 15/13 discipline: one gain value → one timed lap → log it → change once. teams produce a small gain table (gain / lap time / observation) and pick their champion value. vocabulary upgrade: they are tuning a control loop — the same mathematics that keeps drones level and cruise control steady. they should know the thing they built today is not a toy idea. type the p-follower; first run at gain ≈ 0.3 — expect lazy curve-cutting. tuning sprints: gain table with 5+ values, timed laps, one change at a time. champion runs: best gain, three laps, best time recorded next to grade 7’s bang-bang times. on your lesson sheet: your gain table + the value where wobble returned. function names below follow mblock’s cyberpi python api; minor names vary by version — the class rule is: trust the editor’s autocomplete. if the robot flees the line instantly, the offset sign is inverted — flip the +/− and move on. same track and battery across tuning laps, or the table lies. p-follower completes laps visibly smoother than bang-bang gain table with 5+ tested values, one-change discipline wobble-returns gain found, matching the prediction import mbot2, cyberpi

base = 45      # cruise rpm
gain = 0.5     # tune me!

while true:
    err = cyberpi.quad_rgb_sensor.get_offset_track()
    steer = err * gain   # the whole idea
    mbot2.drive_speed(base + steer,
                      base - steer) a champion gain chosen from a table, and the gain at which the wobble returns found and checked against yesterday's prediction. wobble-return gain found and compared against the session 5 prediction champion gain defended from the table rather than from feel

title: Measure It
goal: Claims become graphs: error over time proves proportional beats bang-bang.
label: G9 · S7
text:
claims become graphs: error over time proves proportional beats bang-bang. engineers don’t say “it looks smoother” — they show a graph. today: log the error signal while driving (append offset values to a list, or print them and transcribe), then plot error-vs-time for bang-bang and for p-control. the bang-bang plot is a square wave bouncing between extremes; the p-control plot shrinks and settles. one picture, whole argument. pair it with lap-time data: p-control is usually both smoother and faster — a rare free lunch, and worth noticing. fast teams get the d-term teaser: error × gain still overshoots a little because it reacts to where the robot is, not where it’s heading; adding a term based on how fast error is changing (the derivative) damps that. even implementing nothing, knowing pid exists — and that they built the p — is the doorway out of this course into real control engineering. add error logging to both followers; drive 20 s each, capture the series. plot both series (paper grid or spreadsheet); overlay or side-by-side. compare + write the two-sentence evidence-based conclusion under the graphs. d-term teaser for all; extension pairs may prototype it. transcribing 200 numbers is misery — sample every 5th, or screenshot the console. the conclusion sentence must cite the graph (‘peak error fell from ~90 to ~25’), not vibes. both error-time plots produced from real logged data written conclusion cites numbers from the graphs team can say what the d in pid would add errors = []
for i in range(200):     # ~20 s of driving
    err = cyberpi.quad_rgb_sensor.get_offset_track()
    errors.append(err)
    steer = err * gain
    mbot2.drive_speed(base + steer,
                      base - steer)
    time.sleep(0.1)

print(errors)            # copy out to plot a written conclusion that cites numbers from graphs the team produced out of its own logged data. the written conclusion cites specific figures from the team's own plots the d-term explained in the team's own words, not recited

title: The D Term
goal: A PD follower running, and its overshoot measured against Session 7’s P-only trace.
label: G9 · S8
text:
a pd follower running, and its overshoot measured against session 7’s p-only trace. yesterday’s teaser, cashed in. a p-controller looks only at where the robot is: offset 40 gets the same correction whether the robot is racing back towards the line or drifting further off it. those two situations need opposite treatment, and p cannot tell them apart — which is exactly why the trace still overshoots. the missing information is already in their data: the difference between this reading and the last one. rising error means going the wrong way, push harder; falling error means the correction is already working, ease off. one subtraction, err − last_err, and the controller can finally see motion instead of position. then the discipline that makes it real. freeze kp at session 6’s champion value and change only kd — the one-change rule, now protecting a two-dimensional search that punishes sloppiness fast. two things to predict aloud before anyone runs: too much d makes the robot twitchy rather than wobbly (it amplifies sensor noise, because noise is the fastest-changing thing in the signal), and the loop’s beat is part of the maths — err − last_err means nothing without a fixed interval between reads, so a stray print() inside the loop silently retunes the controller. that is the day’s real lesson and it applies to every control loop they will ever write. add last_err and the delta line to the champion p-follower; run once at kd = 0 and confirm nothing changed. kd sweep: 5+ values with kp frozen, one timed lap each, logged in the table beside session 6’s. re-log the error series at champion kd and overlay it on session 7’s p-only trace: same axes, same run length. on your lesson sheet: the kd at which the robot became twitchy, and what it was reacting to. function names below follow mblock’s cyberpi python api; minor names vary by version — the class rule is: trust the editor’s autocomplete. kd = 0 must behave exactly like session 6. if it does not, the bug is in the new code, not in the theory — find it before sweeping anything. good kd values are often much smaller than kp. start at a tenth of it and work up, or the first run is uninformative violence. nobody adds a print() inside the loop today. log to a list and print after — the sleep is load-bearing now. pd follower runs, and kd = 0 reproduces session 6 exactly kd table with 5+ values, kp frozen throughout overshoot compared against the session 7 trace with numbers import mbot2, cyberpi, time

base = 45      # cruise rpm
kp   = 0.5     # s6's champion, frozen
kd   = 0.0     # the only thing you change

last_err = 0

while true:
    err = cyberpi.quad_rgb_sensor.get_offset_track()
    # delta: how fast the error is changing
    delta = err - last_err
    # p sees where we are, d where we head
    steer = kp * err + kd * delta
    mbot2.drive_speed(base + steer,
                      base - steer)
    last_err = err
    # a fixed beat, or delta means nothing
    time.sleep(0.02) a champion kd defended from a table, and the twitch threshold found rather than avoided. the champion kd chosen from a table with kp frozen in every row the twitch threshold found, and what the robot was reacting to named

title: Dead Reckoning
goal: A calibrated drive_cm() built on the encoders — and the square’s closing error measured over three runs.
label: G9 · S9
text:
a calibrated drive_cm() built on the encoders — and the square’s closing error measured over three runs. the rover has no ultrasonic and no gps. everything it knows about where it is comes from counting how far its own motors have turned, and that is called dead reckoning — the same method that crossed oceans before satellites. the arithmetic is one line: a wheel of diameter d advances π·d for every full turn, so degrees convert to centimetres. but do not compute the constant from the sprocket — measure it. command a long straight, lay a tape measure along what the robot actually did, and divide. theory gives you a number; the floor gives you the right one, and on tracks those two are never the same because rubber slips. then the hard truth, and it is the one the capstone is built on: error accumulates and never cancels. drive a 50 cm square four times round and measure the gap between where the robot started and where it finished — distance and heading, three runs, a spread rather than a number. nothing is broken; skid steering scrubs the tracks sideways on every turn and a little of each turn is simply lost. that spread is the budget every later behaviour must live inside, and it is precisely why the mission ends by stopping on a colour marker rather than by counting centimetres. dead reckoning gets you near. a sensor gets you there. write that sentence on the board and leave it up until session 20. calibration run: command a long straight, measure the real distance with a tape, compute deg_per_cm for this robot on this floor. build drive_cm() closing the loop on the encoder; verify it at 20, 50 and 100 cm against the tape. the square, three times: mark the start pose in tape, measure the closing gap and the heading error each run. on your lesson sheet: your three closing errors, and the one sentence about what a sensor buys you. function names below follow mblock’s cyberpi python api; minor names vary by version — the class rule is: trust the editor’s autocomplete. the rover’s motor cables are crossed, so em1 is not necessarily the side you expect. read the sign once, then let abs() carry it and stop worrying about which is which. every team gets a different deg_per_cm and that is correct. a borrowed constant is the fastest way to lose an afternoon. re-measure on the venue floor before demo day. tile, carpet and a dusty hall are three different constants. low battery changes the answer too. note the charge level next to the number or the calibration expires silently. deg_per_cm measured on this robot, not computed or copied drive_cm() lands within ±2 cm at 20, 50 and 100 cm three square runs with closing distance and heading error recorded import mbot2, cyberpi, time

deg_per_cm = 12.4   # measured, not copied

def turned():
    return abs(mbot2.em_get_angle('em1'))

def drive_cm(cm, speed=40):
    mbot2.em_reset_angle('em1')
    v = speed * (1 if cm > 0 else -1)
    while turned() < abs(cm) * deg_per_cm:
        mbot2.drive_speed(v, v)
        time.sleep(0.01)
    mbot2.em_stop()

for i in range(4):   # the square again
    drive_cm(50)
    mbot2.turn(90) an error budget stated as a number this team measured, and a defended answer to why the mission cannot be built from centimetres alone. the closing error stated as a measured range rather than a single lucky run one mission design the team's own error budget rules out, named

title: The Arms, in Python
goal: Both grip arms moving under Python control, mirrored angles hidden behind a guard that a stranger cannot break.
label: G9 · S10
text: both grip arms moving under python control, mirrored angles hidden behind a guard that a stranger cannot break. the rover already has its arms — they went on in grade 8 and they have not come off. what changes today is that there are two of them and the language is python. start ceremonial: open, hold, close, applause. then meet the problem the second arm creates. the arms are mirror images, on s1 and s2, so "open" is a large angle on one and a small angle on the other — the same physical word, two opposite numbers. that asymmetry is a fact about the metal, and the whole job of today’s code is to make sure no other line in the program ever has to know it. grip_open() knows. nothing else does. then the session’s bigger idea: defensive programming — code that assumes mistakes will happen and contains them. grade 8 measured a safe range and respected it; this year the range is enforced, by a clamp() that every command passes through, so the robot is physically unable to hurt itself no matter what the rest of the file asks for. test it adversarially and out loud: call arm_to(500, -500) on purpose and watch both arms stop quietly at their limits. then hand the robot to another pair and invite them to break it, because a guard that has only been tested by the person who wrote it has not been tested. re-measure both arms by hand, unpowered. grade 8’s numbers are a starting guess, not a constant — a year of use moves them. build clamp() and arm_to(); wrap grip_open() and grip_close() over the mirrored angles; adversarial tests. choreography mini-challenge: a 3-pose salute using only the named verbs, with no raw servo call anywhere in the file. on your lesson sheet: why should the mirror live in one function rather than at every call site? function names below follow mblock’s cyberpi python api; minor names vary by version — the class rule is: trust the editor’s autocomplete. the servo call especially varies — find it together in autocomplete. servos are on s1 and s2 on this robot. s3 and s4 belong to a different build and a program that addresses them moves nothing at all: a silent failure, and worth naming before anyone loses ten minutes to it. if an arm judders at the edges of its range, back both constants off 5°. mechanical margin is wisdom. never force an arm past resistance. the gear teeth strip silently and there are no spares in the box. both arms move to commanded angles through arm_to() only guard proven by adversarial calls from another pair 3-pose salute runs with no raw servo call in the file import mbot2, time # measured by hand on this robot, power off # the arms mirror, so the numbers invert l_shut, l_open = 20, 80 # left arm, s1 r_shut, r_open = 80, 20 # right arm, s2 def clamp(v, a, b): lo, hi = min(a, b), max(a, b) return max(lo, min(hi, v)) # nothing reaches a servo except via here def arm_to(left, right): l = clamp(left, l_shut, l_open) r = clamp(right, r_shut, r_open) mbot2.servo_set(l, 's1') mbot2.servo_set(r, 's2') # the only place the mirror is spelled out def grip_open(): arm_to(l_open, r_open) def grip_close(): arm_to(l_shut, r_shut) grip_open() time.sleep(1) arm_to(500, -500) # clamped to the limits grip_close() a guard that cannot be got round — proved by adversarial calls from someone trying to break it, not by reading the code. another pair failed to break the guard with adversarial calls the limit constant changed in one place and every call site followed

title: Pick & Place
goal: The grip earns its keep: hold a block, carry it through a turn, release it in a zone — a challenge ladder.
label: G9 · S11
text: the grip earns its keep: hold a block, carry it through a turn, release it in a zone — a challenge ladder. the challenge-ladder format: rungs of increasing difficulty, teams climb at their own pace, each rung demoed to the teacher before the next. rung 1: close on a foam block and hold it while the robot is lifted and tilted by hand (grip angle tuning — too loose slips, too tight stalls the servo and heats it). rung 2: grip, drive 30 cm with drive_cm(), release inside a taped zone — arm and motion coordinated, plus the discovery that driving shakes the payload and slower is surer. rung 3: the same delivery with a 90° turn in the middle, released on a target within 3 cm — because a skid-steer turn scrubs sideways and the block rotates in the grip while it does. one mechanical fact shapes the whole ladder and is worth stating before anyone climbs: each arm has exactly one servo, so grip and height are the same number. this robot cannot hold a block at one height and open at another — it releases where it stands. that rules out stacking entirely, and it is not a limitation to apologise for; it is the constraint every mission this year has to be designed around, which is what engineers do with constraints. let the struggle at rung 3 happen — it is genuinely hard and that is its job. the debug discipline carries: one variable per attempt (grip angle or approach speed or turn speed), logged. teams should end today knowing their grip’s personality: what it holds well, where it fumbles. that self-knowledge writes session 12’s failure log. ladder briefing + demo protocol; blocks and zones distributed. climb: grip and hold (r1), carry 30 cm and release (r2), carry through a turn onto a 3 cm target (r3); teacher demos at each rung. standings + lesson sheet: your highest rung and the single change that unlocked it. foam blocks only — wooden ones stall the servos and strip gears on a bad grip. r2 zone generous (a5-size) today; r3 tightens it to a 3 cm target and the capstone tightens it again. a servo held against a block it cannot close on gets hot: if an arm is warm to the touch, the grip angle is too far past contact. back it off 5°. turn slowly while carrying. the block rotates in the grip during the scrub, and that is session 9’s drift showing up in a new costume. rung 2 (carry & release) reached by every team rung 3 attempted with logged one-change attempts grip strengths and weaknesses written down rung 2 reached by every team, and the grip's personality known — what it holds, and the condition under which it lets go. rung 2 reached with the carry-and-release complete the grip's failure stated as a condition, never as "sometimes"

title: Reusable Arm Code
goal: pick(), place(), carry_to() — the mission’s verbs, plus an honest failure log.
label: G9 · S12
text:
pick(), place(), carry_to() — the mission’s verbs, plus an honest failure log. yesterday’s working sequences become a library: pick() (open, close the last centimetres, grip, settle), place() (release, retreat before turning), carry_to(cm) (a slower drive_cm, because a carried block slips). the capstone mission will then read like english: follow_line() … pick() … carry_to(30) … place(). when top-level code reads like the mission description, the decomposition is right — that’s the design smell to teach. note what each verb is really hiding: pick() hides the mirrored servo angles from session 10, carry_to() hides session 9’s calibration constant. three sessions of work, four words of code. second deliverable: the failure log. run pick() twenty times; count successes; describe every failure precisely (‘block rotated in the grip during the turn’, not ‘it dropped it’). an 85% grip is fine — an unknown-% grip is a time bomb in a scored mission. reliability engineering in one lunch-sized lesson: measure it, then decide whether to fix it or design around it (e.g. re-grip attempt on failure — which is session 19’s recovery topic, seeded today). extract pick(), place(), carry_to() from yesterday’s code; parameters where useful. failure log: 20 pick() runs, success count + precise failure notes. library swap-test (the session 2 ritual): another pair runs your pick() cold. on your lesson sheet: your reliability %, and fix-it vs. design-around-it — which will you choose? the sleep after grip_close matters — servos need a beat; its absence is the ghost bug of the week. place() retreats before it turns. skip that and the arms sweep the block out of the zone they just put it in: a bug that looks like a grip failure and is not. failure descriptions must name conditions; ‘sometimes’ is banned vocabulary. pick()/place()/carry_to() pass the swap-test 20-run failure log with precise descriptions a reliability decision made and written down def pick():
    grip_open()
    # creep the last few centimetres
    drive_cm(6, speed=20)
    grip_close()
    time.sleep(0.3)   # servos need a beat

def place():
    grip_open()
    time.sleep(0.2)
    # retreat before turning, or the arms
    # sweep the block out of the zone again
    drive_cm(-8, speed=20)

def carry_to(cm):
    # slower: a carried block slips
    drive_cm(cm, speed=25) a known reliability percentage for pick(), and a written decision about what to do with that number. a reliability percentage measured over 20 runs and stated plainly a fix-it or design-around-it decision written and justified by the number

title: Navigate + Manipulate ✱
goal: The full pipeline in miniature: follow line → detect marker → stop → pick → deliver.
label: G9 · S13
text:
the full pipeline in miniature: follow line → detect marker → stop → pick → deliver. integration day — the capstone in miniature, and deliberately so: line following (session 6) + color-marker detection (grade 7, session 16’s idea, now in python) + arm library (session 12) chained into one mission. the new engineering content is the seams: stopping accurately at the marker (momentum overshoots — the two-speed approach returns yet again), and positioning the arms relative to a block whose location is only as precise as the stop was. errors compound down a pipeline; students meet that truth physically today — and session 9’s measured error budget is the number that predicts how badly. run it as a milestone session: the pipeline working once, even slowly and inelegantly, is the win. teams that get a clean run should immediately answer the harder question: how repeatable? three runs in a row is the real bar — and the gap between ‘worked once’ and ‘works reliably’ is the theme of the entire build-sprint unit ahead. whiteboard the pipeline; identify the two seams (stop accuracy, arm alignment). build and iterate; markers and blocks on the standard course; one-change discipline at the seams. milestone attempts: pipeline end-to-end; then repeatability count (n clean of 3). at_marker() and follow_step() are the class’s own helpers, not library calls — the top-level mission is nine lines because three sessions of work are hiding behind those two names. point at that. buffer session — a struggling class can pre-place the block at a fixed, known stop point. slow the base speed near expected markers; detection at speed is flaky and that’s a real sensor lesson. full pipeline ran end-to-end at least once both seams named with their observed failure mode repeatability measured (n of 3), whatever the n # the marker is red, under the l1 probe
while not at_marker():
    follow_step()   # the tuned pd loop, s8
mbot2.em_stop()

pick()
mbot2.turn(180)
carry_to(40)
place()
celebrate()        # s2, still earning the pipeline measured for repeatability, with both seams named and their failure modes characterised. repeatability measured as n of 3 and recorded honestly both seams described with the conditions that trigger them

title: Design Sprint
goal: Each team’s capstone mission fully specified, scoped and signed off.
label: G9 · S15
text: each team’s capstone mission fully specified, scoped and signed off. the brief, in full: design an autonomous mission simulating a real job — warehouse sorting, rescue supply delivery, harvesting, waste collection, or the team’s own pitch. the robot must navigate (line or programmed path), detect a target (marker/color), manipulate (pick and deliver at least one object) — fully autonomously. demo day (session 20): scored runs plus a 5-minute pitch that must include one honest failure story. today produces four artifacts, in order: problem statement (what real job, why it matters — the pitch’s backbone); success criteria (measurable: ‘delivers 2 blocks to zones in course sketch (top-down, dimensions, line path, marker and zone positions); task breakdown mapped onto sessions 1–14 (every task should point at a session where its skill was built — anything pointing nowhere is scope risk, cut it or flag it). the sign-off gate is strictest of all three years: ambition is celebrated, unscoped ambition is returned for revision. ‘impressive and finished’ beats ‘amazing and imaginary’ — write it on the board. brief + rubric + example missions pitched fast (steal-able starting points). problem statement + success criteria drafted; criteria must contain numbers. course sketch + task breakdown with session references. sign-off interviews: scope probe (‘which task is riskiest? what’s your cut line?’). ban criteria without numbers — ‘works well’ is not a criterion. require a written cut line: the feature they’ll drop first if time runs short. deciding it now removes the mid-sprint agony. all four artifacts complete; criteria numeric every task maps to a source session cut line written; sign-off passed a mission specified in numbers, with the cut line decided while nobody is yet under any pressure. every success criterion contains a number a stranger could check the cut line written down before any time pressure exists

title: Build Sprint I ✱
goal: Navigation milestone: the robot completes its course path end-to-end, reliably.
label: G9 · S16
text: navigation milestone: the robot completes its course path end-to-end, reliably. sprint rules, borrowed from real teams: a 2-minute standup at the top (each team: done / doing / blocked — blockers get teacher attention first), then heads-down build, then a milestone check at the end. today’s milestone for everyone regardless of mission: navigation end-to-end — the robot travels its full course path and stops where the mission needs it, three times in a row. hold the line on order: teams itching to get the arms working show first that the robot can reliably arrive. navigation is the foundation every later behavior stands on; a wobbly foundation makes every arm bug ambiguous (‘did the grip fail or did we stop 4 cm short?’). reliability before features — it’s the sprint’s only commandment. standup circle: done / doing / blocked; blockers triaged. build: course laid out to the sketch’s dimensions; navigation tuned on the real course. milestone check: 3 consecutive end-to-end navigation runs, witnessed and logged. buffer session: teams behind on p-control tuning catch up here — that is their navigation work. courses on the floor get shuffled between sessions; photograph the layout with a tape measure in frame. 3 consecutive clean navigation runs on the team’s own course standup done in under 2 minutes with a real blocked-list course layout photographed for exact rebuild navigation that arrives reliably three times running, on a course the team can rebuild exactly from its own photograph. three consecutive clean navigation runs witnessed by another team the course rebuilt from a photograph with dimensions visible

title: Build Sprint II + Code Review
goal: Manipulation development advances — and every team’s code survives a peer review.
label: G9 · S17
text: manipulation development advances — and every team’s code survives a peer review. build continues (arm behaviors onto the navigation spine), but the hour’s signature event is the cross-team code review — the professional practice, scaled down. pairs of teams swap tablets and read each other’s code against a four-line checklist: functions with clear names? · constants instead of magic numbers? · comments that say why? · no copy-pasted near-duplicates? reviewers write two ‘strengths’ and two ‘suggestions’ — the discipline of kind precision. frame it before anyone reads a line: review is about the code, not the coder; every suggestion is a gift that saves a future debugging hour. the checklist is the capstone rubric’s code-quality section verbatim — so today is a free mock exam. teams then get sprint time to act on what review found; acting on feedback is the half of the skill that classrooms usually skip. standup + review protocol and the four-line checklist. cross-team review: read, checklist, write 2 strengths + 2 suggestions. sprint: apply at least one review suggestion, then continue manipulation build. milestone pulse: where is each team vs. the plan? cut lines re-checked aloud. model one review comment style first: ‘pick() is very readable’ / ‘gain=0.5 appears 3× — constant?’ a team ‘too busy to review’ is the team that most needs it — the checklist takes 12 minutes, hold firm. review exchanged: 2+2 written comments per team at least one suggestion applied the same hour manipulation visibly progressed on the mission course code that survives a stranger reading it against the rubric's own checklist, with at least one suggestion applied the same hour. two strengths and two suggestions written, and the same received at least one suggestion applied within the hour, not deferred

title: Build Sprint III
goal: Full mission integration: navigation + manipulation attempts on the complete course.
label: G9 · S18
text: full mission integration: navigation + manipulation attempts on the complete course. integration week peaks: manipulation joins navigation and full mission attempts begin. expect the seam bugs from session 13 at mission scale — stop accuracy vs. arm alignment — plus the new one: cumulative drift over a longer course (small navigation errors sum; missions that pick early and deliver late feel it most). the state-machine structure from session 14 earns its keep now: teams with clean states can add a re-align step to one state without touching the rest. keep a visible run log per team on the wall: attempt number, phases completed, failure point. the log turns frustration into data — ‘we fail at delivery 3 of 4 times’ is actionable; ‘it keeps breaking’ is despair. it also quietly writes the failure-story half of the pitch. teams at their cut line make the cut today, without shame — point at the board from session 15. standup; run-log sheets posted per team. full mission attempts; every attempt logged; fixes between runs follow one-change discipline. milestone: at least one full-mission success, or the cut executed and the reduced mission succeeding. enforce the log — memory lies under sprint pressure, paper doesn’t. battery sag changes stop distance late in the hour; note battery level in the log too (grade 7 wisdom, still true). full mission completed at least once (original or post-cut scope) run log with phase-level failure data one drift/seam fix implemented via a single state change a phase-level run log that turns frustration into data, and one seam or drift fix made through a single change. the dominant failure point identified from the log rather than from memory every between-run fix was a single logged change

title: Rehearsal & Pitch Prep ✱
goal: Failure recovery hardened, run configuration frozen, and the 5-minute pitch rehearsed.
label: G9 · S19
text: failure recovery hardened, run configuration frozen, and the 5-minute pitch rehearsed. two workstreams. robot: rehearse under demo-day conditions (official start, audience noise simulated, two attempts) and add cheap recovery where the run log points — the classics: re-grip once if pick fails (session 12’s seed sprouts), re-find line if lost (grade 7’s search behavior returns), timeout-and-skip rather than freeze forever. then freeze the configuration — the grade 7 race-config ritual, now second nature. pitch (5 minutes, strict): the problem (30 s) → the solution & how it works (2′) → live demo (90 s) → one honest failure story and what it taught (1′). the failure story is mandatory and rubric-weighted — it’s where engineering maturity shows, and after three years of debug discipline every team has a good one. rehearse with a timer; cutting to fit five minutes is itself the exercise. assign demo roles: driver (starts the run), narrator (talks over it), catcher (handles the robot if chaos wins). recovery pass: implement the top recovery the run log justifies; verify it triggers correctly. freeze: race configuration written, code committed, no edits after this line. pitch rehearsal ×2 with timer; peers give one keep / one cut note. demo-day logistics: order drawn, roles assigned, batteries on chargers. buffer session: recovery can shrink to timeout-and-skip only — but the freeze and the timed rehearsal are untouchable. the failure story must end on the lesson, not the excuse — coach the last sentence. one recovery behavior demonstrably triggers and works configuration frozen in writing pitch fits 5:00 with all four parts, twice one recovery behaviour that demonstrably triggers, a configuration frozen in writing, and a pitch that fits five minutes twice running. the recovery fires when the failure is caused deliberately the pitch fits 5:00 twice, with all four parts present both times

title: Demo Day
goal: Scored autonomous runs, real pitches, and a three-year retrospective that lands.
label: G9 · S20
text: scored autonomous runs, real pitches, and a three-year retrospective that lands. run it as the event three years earned: audience seated (invite classes, teachers, parents if possible), visible scoreboard (phase points per team’s own success criteria + small style bonus), two attempts each with pit time between, pitches delivered from the front. the teacher’s job today is master of ceremonies — the students carry the content, and they can. close the arc deliberately. the retrospective ritual: the session 1/grade 7 question projected (‘what is a robot?’) — let them answer it again, now with three years of hands. then the pathways talk, concrete and short: what they built maps to real fields — control engineering (their p-controller), ml engineering (their mirror), embedded software (their guard functions), robotics competitions, and the kit’s 30+ module ecosystem for a robotics club afterlife. end on the honest sentence: they didn’t learn about robotics — they did robotics, sixty hours of it. setup: courses rebuilt from photos, scoreboard up, order posted, audience seated. the event: per team — pitch (5′ incl. live demo) with scored attempts; pit repairs allowed between rounds. awards: precision, engineering, comeback, audience choice. retrospective question + pathways + the closing sentence. rebuild courses from the tape-measure photos — ‘the course moved’ is a heartbreak with a known cure. score against each team’s own success criteria — missions differ; fairness lives in the spec they signed. every team: two scored attempts + a complete 5-minute pitch failure stories told and applauded scoreboard archived; three-year arc closed scored runs against each team's own signed criteria, pitches with the failure story told, and the three-year question answered again. every team scored against its own signed success criteria the grade 7 question answered again, with evidence of how the answer changed

title: Build it — chassis, motors, wheels
goal: The bottom half of a robot, built by reading pictures.
label: G7 · Step 1
text: chassis, motors and wheels assembled correctly, straight from the printed guide. the bottom half of a robot, built by reading pictures. reading an exploded diagram the mbot2 guide is almost wordless, and that is deliberate: reading an exploded diagram is an engineering skill in itself. three things to find in every picture before touching a screwdriver — which parts, which way round they go, and which screws. the screw lengths are drawn actual size in the margin; hold yours against the page. the single most common error in this build is a motor mounted backwards, or the left and right motor cables swapped. neither shows up until the robot drives — and then it turns when you told it to go straight. so there is a rule: no wheels go on until another team has checked the orientation. open the box over a tray and sort the screws by size. this is the single biggest time-saver of the day, and the teams who skip it will be hunting for an m4×8 in twenty minutes. read one diagram together — guide step ② on the screen. name the parts, the orientation and the screws out loud before anyone builds anything. build guide steps ①–③: motor cables in first, motors into the chassis with m4×8, wheel hubs pressed into the tyres, wheels onto the shafts with m2.5×12. cross-team check before the wheels go on: another team confirms both motors face the way the diagram shows and the cables run where they can still be reached. spin both wheels by hand. they should turn freely and sound the same as each other. on your lesson sheet: one diagram that was confusing, and how you worked it out. plug each motor cable in before the motor goes into the chassis. the port is unreachable afterwards, and every year a team takes a motor back out to discover this. the four long m4×25 screws belong to the next step. a team reaching for them today is on the wrong page. snug, not tight. these screws go into plastic and they will strip. half-built is fine. label the tray with the team name and put it on the shelf. both motors mounted, orientation checked and signed off by another team wheels spin freely and quietly by hand no leftover screws that nobody can name

title: Finish it — sensors, shield, first power-on
goal: A robot that is yours, checked by somebody else, and switched on.
label: G7 · Step 2
text: a finished robot that another team has inspected and signed off, powered on for the first time. a robot that is yours, checked by somebody else, and switched on. quality control before it matters finish the build: the two sensors underneath and in front, then the mbot2 shield on top — its battery is built in, so charge it before this lesson — and the cyberpi last. cables go in with the 10 cm mbuild leads; the guide crosses the 20 cm one out in red, and a cable left loose near a wheel is the commonest cause of a robot that "randomly stops" in week nine. then quality control, which is a real engineering practice and not a tidying-up ritual. each team inspects another team's robot against four points and signs it. you stop seeing your own mistakes after twenty minutes with a screwdriver; somebody else sees them in ten seconds. everything the class finds today is a fault that does not eat a lesson later. em means encoder motor. em1 and em2 are the two numbered motor ports on the shield — they are not different kinds of motor. a block that says em1 controls whichever motor cable is plugged into port em1, and likewise for em2. on this standard mbot2 build, connect the left motor to em1 and the right motor to em2; that lets later blocks use those names to choose a wheel. a port contains several electrical pins. s1 and s2 are multifunction connectors; each has separate contacts for power, ground and a signal. a digital-read block looks only at the signal voltage relative to ground and turns it into a yes/no answer: near ground is low / false, and near the positive logic supply is high / true. in a common pull-down switch circuit, open is low and closing the switch makes it high. some sensors are active-low and reverse that meaning, so their documentation wins. a signal with nothing connected can float unpredictably and is not a valid reading. this course does not wire custom circuits to those pins, but those words explain what the raw s1/s2 pin blocks in the palette are reading. fit the underside and the front: quad rgb sensor and mini wheel below (m4×14), ultrasonic sensor at the front (m4×14). the ultrasonic must face exactly forward — a small tilt gives nonsense readings for the rest of the year. shield on with the four long m4×25 screws, cyberpi slides in last. route the cables and tuck them where no wheel can reach them. read the port labels as you connect the motors: em means encoder motor; left motor → em1 and right motor → em2. cross-team qc. four points, inspected on somebody else's robot and signed: wheels turn freely · cables tucked · battery seated · nothing rattles when shaken. fix whatever qc found on your own robot. then shake it and spin the wheels in front of the class. power on for the first time. it lights up and shows the makeblock screen — that is all it does yet, and that is the point: the robot exists, and next step you make it yours. name the robot and label it. on your lesson sheet: what did qc catch on the robot you inspected? the ultrasonic sensor must face exactly forward. sight down it from above before tightening. 10 cm cables for the sensors. teams reaching for the 20 cm one are on the step the guide crossed out. left motor into em1, right into em2. swapped means the robot turns when told to go straight, and you will not find out until step 3. the shield's battery is built in and charges over usb-c. start every build day charged. label each robot with its team name now, while there is still one on the bench that is not labelled. the robot passes all four qc points, signed by another team sensors mounted straight and plugged into the right ports it powers on, and the team knows whose robot it is

title: Hello, robot
goal: A robot that introduces itself on power-up and plays back your own recorded voice.
label: G7 · Step 3
text: the robot switches on and greets the class by itself, with no tablet attached — and answers its two buttons differently. a robot that introduces itself on power-up and plays back your own recorded voice. sequence · event there are two ways to run a program, and this year you normally use upload. in upload mode mblock translates your blocks and sends the whole program into the robot; it then runs by itself with the computer disconnected. in live mode the program runs on the computer and sends commands to the connected robot, so mblock must stay open and the robot stops when the connection drops. upload is like handing someone a written recipe and leaving the kitchen; live is standing beside them dictating each step. prove the difference by unplugging the cable at the end of this lesson. a program is a list of instructions that run in order. that is a sequence, and swapping two lines changes what happens — which students should do once, on purpose, in the first ten minutes. nothing runs until something starts it. that is an event. on this robot there is no green flag and no keyboard: it starts itself with when cyberpi starts up, or you press button a or b on the robot. say this out loud today, because everything else this year depends on it — the robot has no stage. if you want to see something, you put it on its screen. connect: add device mbot2, choose upload mode, and run a one-block test (an led flash) before trusting anything else. anyone whose device says cyberpi has the wrong robot — they will have no motors later. sequence: on start-up, show your team name and light the leds. then swap two blocks and run it again. write down what changed — that is the whole idea of order. your voice: start recording, say something, stop recording, then play it back when button a is pressed. the robot is now yours. two buttons, two behaviours. predict out loud what b will do before pressing it. then make the ultrasonic sensor's eyes show an emotion to match. make it yours: name, colour, sound, face. show the robot to another team without touching their table. unplug the usb and press the button. it still works — that is upload mode, and it is why nobody is tethered to a tablet this year. device check, before anything else. this course needs mblock with an mbot2 device. that works on an android tablet in chrome at ide.mblock.cc — and nowhere else. an ipad cannot run it in any browser, and the mblock mobile apps on both ios and android support only the original mbot, not the mbot2. sort this out before the first lesson, not during it. the device must be mbot2. if a team picked cyberpi they will get through today happily and hit a wall in step 4 when there are no motion blocks — check every screen now. recording overwrites the previous one. agree a signal for "recording now" or twelve robots record each other. there is no green flag on a robot. teams who ask where it is have understood the question — answer it with when cyberpi starts up. the greeting runs from power-on with no cable attached buttons a and b do visibly different things the team can say why the robot has no green flag and no stage every robot's device is set to mbot2, not cyberpi when cyberpi starts up set print size to big print team rocket and move to a newline led all displays r 0 g 128 b 255 play led animation rainbow until done when button a pressed play recording ultrasonic 2 1 displays emotion happy when button b pressed clear screen print bye! turn off led all

title: Commanded, and actual
goal: A robot that parks in a taped garage and shows what it thinks it did.
label: G7 · Step 4
text: the robot drives a distance you asked for, and the team can say — with numbers — how far off it really was and why. a robot that parks in a taped garage and shows what it thinks it did. motion · commanded vs actual moves forward 100 cm until done does not guess. the motors are encoder motors: they count how far they have turned, and the block stops when the count says 100 cm. the robot has been measuring itself all along. contrast power with position. a command such as 50% power is like holding an accelerator halfway down: it says how strongly to drive a motor, not how fast it will actually go or where it should stop. battery, friction and load all change the resulting speed. a plain dc motor has no sensor, so it cannot accept an angle — it simply keeps spinning until another block stops it. an encoder motor can accept a distance or angle because its sensor counts the rotation and gives the controller feedback about when the target has been reached. the plain-motor block has an m1 / m2 / all menu. m1 controls the added dc motor plugged into extension port m1; m2 controls the one in port m2; all sends the same command to both ports at once. do not confuse these with em1 / em2, which are the encoder-motor ports used by the two driving wheels: m means a plain extension motor, while em means encoder motor. so there are three numbers today, not one: what you asked for, what the ruler says, and what the robot thinks it did. when they disagree — and they will, because of wheel slip, battery level and floor surface — that gap is not a mistake. it is information, and every tuning decision for the rest of the year comes out of it. add one drive block to yesterday's greeting. park the robot on the start line and send it 100 cm. three runs, same code. measure each with a ruler and write all three down — not just the best one. they will differ, and that is the point. change one thing: a different floor, or a lower speed. three more runs. which change mattered more? put the robot's own count on the screen beside your ruler number. now you can see what it believes versus what is true. class data on the board. same code, same floor, different robots — who drifted most? argue about why. log the table. it is the reference every time the robot misbehaves this year. tape the start line. "it worked last time" is nearly always a different starting spot. note the battery level beside each run. a robot that has driven all morning undershoots, and teams who do not record it will blame their code. do not let anyone average the three runs into one number yet. the spread is the finding. three runs measured with a ruler and all three recorded the robot's own count is on screen next to the measured distance the team can name one physical reason commanded and actual differ when cyberpi starts up set print size to big print team rocket and move to a newline led all displays r 0 g 128 b 255 play led animation rainbow until done when button a pressed play recording ultrasonic 2 1 displays emotion happy when button b pressed clear screen print bye! turn off led all when joystick middle pressed reset encoder motor (1) em1 rotated angle moves forward 100 cm until done show label 1 join robot says: (encoder motor (1) em1 rotated angle (°)) at x: 0 y: 0 by small pixel

title: Stop copying blocks
goal: A shape machine: change two numbers, get any polygon.
label: G7 · Step 5
text:
the robot drives any closed shape the teacher names, from one repeat block, first try. a shape machine: change two numbers, get any polygon. loop — repeat build the square the long way first — drive, turn, drive, turn, eight blocks — because the ache of dragging the eighth block is the argument for what comes next. then replace all eight with repeat 4 wrapped round two. same behaviour, less code, and one place to change it. the turn is the outside angle, not the inside one. walk it: at each corner of a square you turn 90°, and after four corners you have turned all the way round — 360°. so for any closed shape, each turn is 360 ÷ sides. let teams try 60° for a triangle first and watch it spiral; the failure teaches the rule faster than the rule does. build the square with no loop. count the blocks. complain. rebuild it with repeat 4. prove the behaviour is identical by running both and watching. triangle. predict the turn angle first and write it down. if you wrote 60, run it anyway — the spiral is worth seeing. any polygon: put the division into the block itself so one program draws a pentagon, a hexagon, an octagon by changing one number. closing contest: the shape whose end point is nearest its start wins. measure the gap with a ruler. log the rule in your own words, with a drawing. step 19 turns that rule into a block of your own. slow turns close better than fast ones. a team that lowers the speed will beat a team that does not, and noticing that is half the lesson. teams who reach for a variable here have invented step 13 early. let them, and say so. 60° for the triangle is the most productive wrong answer in the course. do not prevent it. the square runs from a repeat block, behaviour unchanged the triangle turns 120°, derived rather than told a shape the team had not tried closes on the first attempt when cyberpi starts up

title: It runs by itself
goal: A robot that drives until it sees the red strip, backs away, turns, and continues patrolling until you stop it.
label: G7 · Step 6
text: a patrol that starts on button a, stays inside the red-tape arena by sensing its boundary, and runs until stopped without a tablet. a robot that drives until it sees the red strip, backs away, turns, and continues patrolling until you stop it. forever · start and stop repeat 4 counts and ends. forever never does. that is the whole difference, and it matters more than it sounds: a robot that is meant to keep watching the world needs a loop with no end, and every autonomous behaviour for the rest of the year sits inside one. something must be able to stop it. stop all on button b is today's answer — a second event, doing the opposite of the first. from now on every program a team writes should be startable and stoppable without touching a cable. a measured distance cannot describe this arena because the robot may start anywhere. let the robot move while its downward-facing quad rgb sensor watches the floor. wait until red makes the tape—not a guessed number of centimetres—the signal to stop, back away, and turn. reversing first clears the strip so the next loop does not detect the same edge again. take the square from step 5 and wrap it in forever. watch it never stop. then explain why fixed 30 cm sides cannot keep it inside the arena when it starts from a different place. build the arena patrol: move forward at 30 rpm, wait until the l1 probe sees red, stop, reverse 5 cm, and turn right 90°. put that sequence inside forever. start near the middle, pointing toward an edge—not on top of the tape. add the stop: button b ends everything. test it while the robot is moving, not while it is parked. unplug and run it inside the red-tape arena for two minutes. if it crosses an edge, lower the speed, check that the sensor points straight down, and confirm that l1 reports red over the tape. log: which of your programs so far could run with no tablet in the room? all of them should. nothing moves until button a is pressed. uploading starts the program on the robot immediately, and a robot that drives the instant it is flashed ends up on the floor — so every program whose start-up script drives now shows press a to start and waits. it is the same idea as this lesson's stop button, one step earlier: a human decides when it begins, and a human decides when it ends. clear a floor area. a forever loop on a table is a robot on the floor thirty seconds later. test the colour reading before the full run: hold the robot safely, place l1 over the floor and then over the tape, and watch the boolean block change. reflections or a sensor mounted too high can make red detection unreliable. agree a volume cap before twelve robots discover the speaker. if a team's stop button does nothing, their stop is inside the forever loop instead of beside it — a genuinely useful bug to let them find. the patrol runs unplugged from a and remains inside the red-tape arena at every edge it detects red, backs away, turns, and continues button b stops it mid-movement, every time the team can say when to use forever and when to use repeat when cyberpi starts up set print size to big print team rocket and move to a newline led all displays r 0 g 128 b 255 play led animation rainbow until done show label 1 press a to start at x: 0 y: 0 by small pixel wait until button a pressed? title: Checkpoint 1 — sequence, event, loop
goal: Nothing new. The class arrives at the same place.
label: G7 · CP 7
text: every student can start a program three ways, order instructions deliberately, and use a loop — before anyone moves to stage b. nothing new. the class arrives at the same place. catch-up gate a buffer hour is available here and is deliberately not in the timetable above — add it only if the class is not level. the stated hours are what the course takes when nobody needs catching up. if the class is level, spend it on the extension: coaches take a program where one number changes the shape, the speed and the colour at once. this is a gate, not a test. nobody moves on until the class is level, because stage b builds directly on all three ideas and a student who is shaky on loops will be lost inside two steps. run it as three hands-on challenges, not a written paper. students who clear all three become coaches — and coaching is not doing it for them: hands off the other team's robot, questions only. a student who can get someone else there understands it better than one who just finished first. explain the gate and the coaching rule. nobody is behind; the class moves together. the three challenges, in any order, demonstrated to the teacher or to a coach: (1) make the robot do three things in an order you chose, then swap two and predict what changes. (2) start the same program three different ways — power-up, button a, button b. (3) draw a shape the teacher names, using a loop, first try. pairing: everyone who cleared all three takes one student who has not. hands off the robot, questions only. resist letting fast teams race ahead into stage b. the gate only works if it holds. if more than a third of the class is stuck on the same thing, it is a teaching problem, not a student problem — reteach it to everyone rather than pairing round it. write down who coached whom. over four checkpoints the pattern tells you a lot about the class. every student demonstrated all three challenges every student who was behind was coached by a peer, not rescued by an adult the class starts stage b together

title: What the robot can feel
goal: A dashboard the robot carries with it.
label: G7 · Step 8
text:
an instrument panel on the robot's own screen showing every sensor at once, updating live. a dashboard the robot carries with it. sensors as live values every sensor answers with a number, all the time, whether you look or not. distance in centimetres, light as a level, loudness as a level. today the robot stops being something you command and starts being something that knows things. there is no watcher window, so you build the panel yourself — and there are three ways to show a number, which is a real choice. print scrolls, so it is right for a log you want to read backwards. show label overwrites in place, so it is right for a live value. a line chart shows history, so it is right when the shape over time matters more than the number now. join glues a word to a number so a reading says what it is. one sensor, one label: distance on the screen, updating forever. wave your hand at it. add light and loudness on their own lines. use join so each reading is labelled — a bare number on a screen is useless in a month. add the line chart for distance. walk towards the robot slowly and watch the trace. now walk quickly. the chart shows something the number cannot. sensor limits lab: how close before distance stops making sense? how far? what does a soft jumper read compared with a book? record it. swap robots with another team and read their panel. if you cannot tell what a number means, their labels need work. log the limits table. step 9 depends on knowing where the sensor lies. use show label rather than print for live values, or the screen scrolls too fast to read and students conclude the sensor is broken. below about 4 cm and beyond about 3 m the distance reading goes strange. let teams find those edges themselves rather than announcing them. soft and angled surfaces scatter the echo. a jumper is a genuinely different reading from a book, and that is a real sensor lesson, not a fault. three sensors visible at once, each labelled, updating live a line chart that visibly responds to movement a written note of where the distance sensor stops being trustworthy when cyberpi starts up

title: The first decision
goal: A robot that will not crash.

title: Design a job worth doing

text: a signed mission spec whose success criteria contain numbers, and whose every task names a block the team already owns. a specification, and nothing else. specifying with numbers design a job a real robot might do: sort by colour, deliver between two zones, fetch on command, patrol and report. it must navigate, manipulate something with the arm, and take an instruction from a person — voice or controller, your choice. the spec has to be measurable.
